Coquerel's sifaka, Propithecus coquereli, is a folivorous primate endemic to the dry deciduous forests of northwestern Madagascar, exhibiting a life history strategy characterized by slow development and extended parental investment. Neonates of this species are relatively well-developed at birth, with field studies documenting a wet weight at birth of 110 grams [Wwb = 110 grams], though reported values range between 85 and 115 grams depending on maternal condition and litter size. This birth mass is modest compared to the adult body size the animal will eventually achieve. The gestation period that precedes this birth event lasts 162 days [tg = 162 days], a value obtained under the typical body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] measured in resting adults. This gestational duration is consistent with that of other indriids of similar body mass and reflects the relatively slow pace of prenatal development observed across the family. The single infant is then carried ventrally for the first several weeks, clinging to the mother's fur, and begins to sample solid foods after a few months of exclusive lactation, a transition that marks the beginning of the weaning process. Maternal investment during this period is substantial, as the infant is entirely dependent on milk for its early growth and thermoregulation, which imposes considerable energetic costs on the lactating female.

The extended period of maternal care culminates in weaning, a critical developmental milestone that marks the onset of nutritional independence for the juvenile sifaka. Comprehensive studies following marked individuals in the Ankarafantsika National Park indicate that weaning occurs at 150 days [tx = 150 days] after birth, at which point the young animal has achieved a wet weight at weaning of approximately 1000 grams [Wwx = approximately 1000 grams] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This body mass represents a nearly tenfold increase from birth weight, reflecting the rapid early growth phase supported by the mother's milk. The age at weaning was recorded at the species' typical core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], which is maintained throughout this developmental period. After weaning, the juvenile continues to associate closely with its mother for several additional months, learning arboreal foraging techniques and social behaviors, but it must now meet its own daily energetic requirements through the ingestion of leaves, fruits, and flowers. This gradual transition to an independent diet is typical of primates with a slow life history, as the young animal must acquire a complex foraging repertoire before it can survive without maternal assistance in a seasonally challenging environment.

Following the attainment of nutritional independence, the juvenile enters a prolonged sub-adult phase characterized by continued somatic growth and the eventual onset of reproductive maturation. In Coquerel's sifaka, the time since birth at puberty is approximately 2 years [tp = approximately 2 years], a milestone that was confirmed by longitudinal observations at the Duke Lemur Center conducted at the standard body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This age marks the onset of gonadal activity, yet social and physical constraints often delay actual breeding for several more years, as individuals must establish a position within a dominance hierarchy and reach full adult body size. The extended sub-adult period is a common feature among indriids and is thought to reflect the time required to acquire the complex social knowledge and physical strength necessary for successful reproduction in a multi-male, multi-female group structure. During this period, the growing animal continues to increase in body mass, eventually approaching the ultimate size of a mature adult, and begins to engage in play-fighting and scent-marking behaviors that are precursors to adult social interactions. The relatively late puberty contributes to the species' slow life history pace and low maximum reproductive rate.

The adult body size of Propithecus coquereli is moderate for a lemur, with individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 4300 grams [Wwi = 4300 grams] under favorable conditions, although field populations often average between 3.7 and 4.3 kilograms. This sizable body mass supports the species' largely folivorous diet, which requires a capacious digestive tract for efficient fermentation of fibrous plant material. The maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals is 30 years [am = 30 years], measured at the typical body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], a longevity that is among the highest recorded for any lemur species and aligns with the slow life history strategy characteristic of the Indriidae. Older individuals in the population exhibit signs of reproductive senescence and tooth wear, which eventually limit their ability to process tough leaves, contributing to natural mortality. The combination of a long lifespan, late sexual maturation, and a low annual reproductive output places this species firmly at the slow end of the primate life history continuum, making it particularly vulnerable to demographic perturbations such as habitat fragmentation and hunting pressure.

Basal metabolic measurements provide insight into the energetic underpinnings of this slow-paced life history. Respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive adults maintained at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 1012.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 1012.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic expenditure is relatively low when scaled to body mass compared with many other primates, a pattern consistent with the species' arboreal folivory and the energy-conserving lifestyle imposed by a low-quality, high-fiber diet. Reflecting this slow metabolic and life history pace, the maximum reproductive rate is correspondingly modest. Females typically produce a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter], and inter-birth intervals are long, resulting in approximately 1 litter per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 litter per year]. This low annual reproductive output is typical of indriids and constrains the species' capacity for rapid population recovery after disturbance. The integration of these physiological and reproductive data underscores the tightly coupled energetic and demographic strategies that define the life history of this charismatic Malagasy primate.
